blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: The software licence types and how to justify one for a situation; and Artificial Intelligence, its applications and its impact.

blocks.heading: The licence types
blocks.text: Copyright belongs to the maker by default, and a software licence is the maker's statement of what a user may do. Four types cover the field. Free software, in the Free Software Foundation's sense, gives freedom rather than a price: the licence grants the freedom to run the software for any purpose, to study how it works, to change it and to share it and share changes, so the source code comes with it. Open-source software, in the Open Source Initiative's sense, makes the source available under terms that allow use, change and redistribution - the practical terms overlap with free software's, while the stated philosophy differs: free software speaks of users' rights as a principle, open-source speaks of a way of building good software. Shareware is free to try: the user installs and uses it for a trial period, and payment is expected if it is kept, with the source typically closed, so the trying is of the finished tool. Commercial software is sold for a fee with the source kept closed: the vendor's business is the software itself, and the licence permits use, not inspection or redistribution. Freeware stands outside the list as a warning: software free of charge is not the same as free software, because freeware carries no right to see or change the source - 'free' in free software is freedom, not a price.

blocks.heading: Justifying a licence for a situation
blocks.text: The licence is justified by what the situation needs, and two questions do the matching. Who can maintain the system? A school with keen programmers and no budget takes free or open-source software for its website: the source is available to change and share, the programmers restyle and extend it themselves, and no licence fee weighs on the club-rate budget. A firm with a payroll system and no software department takes commercial software: the vendor holds the system under a support contract, so a fault at month end is the vendor's paid problem, and someone is answerable for the mending. What must the software answer to? Work that must be inspected - a public body's counting system, say - leans towards the open licence, because anyone can check the code. Each licence's weakness is the other's strength: open upkeep rests on the user's skills or the community's goodwill, so a small business without those skills inherits the desk the licence leaves the work on; commercial mending comes under a contract and is charged for, so the firm pays in fees what the school pays in skills. Shareware fills the small-tool gap: try the tool on the real job, pay if it stays.

blocks.heading: Artificial Intelligence
blocks.text: Artificial Intelligence is the making of systems that perform tasks that normally need human intelligence: recognising speech and images, translating between languages, learning from data, making judgements. The applications are ordinary now - a phone that turns speech into text, a clinic system that flags suspicious images for a clinician to examine, a route planner that reads traffic - and each application leans on the human around it, which is where the ethics enters. An AI system's judgement affects people: who gets flagged, what a diagnosis suggests, whose face a camera names, and a judgement made by a system is still a professional's act somewhere, so the responsibility does not disappear into the software. The impact runs on three sides. Social: decisions that affect people are made faster and at scale, so the system's fairness matters to many people at once. Economic: work shifts - fewer hours reading every image, more hours on the flagged ones - so some work displaces while new work appears, and the professional's own judgement is part of what is redistributed. Environmental: the systems that learn from large amounts of data are built and run with power and resources, so the asking price of the judgements includes a resource bill. The professional's question is the whole of it: not only whether the system works, but whom it works on and what it costs.

blocks.heading: Common errors
blocks.text: The recurring slip is flattening free software into freeware. Freeware is free of charge, with the source closed and no right to change it; free software (Free Software Foundation) carries the freedom to run, study, change and share the source, whatever it costs. The test: can you see and change the source code? Then it is free software, not just freeware.

blocks.heading: Where this connects
blocks.text: The licences are copyright's instruments, resting on 7.1.1's right. The data AI learns from is the data of 6.1 and 6.2, and the programs it runs are the programs of 9 and 11.
